newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK consumer credit hits record high in June.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK consumer credit hits record high in June.

text.p: British consumer borrowing leapt by 1.275 billion pounds ($2.1 billion) in June, the highest monthly rise since records began in 1993, the Bank of England said on Tuesday.

The jump in credit scotched any idea that personal borrowing would tail off as billions of pounds in building society windfalls are paid out and suggested that frenzied consumer spending continues unabated, economists said.
Not only did consumer credit soar last month but borrowing in May was revised up to 1.23 billion pounds from 1.1 billion.

"There is little in these figures to suggest that the windfalls received from the conversion of the Alliance and Leicester and the Halifax over the last couple of months have dampened consumers' appetite for credit," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Several of Britain's building societies have converted to banks and floated on the stock exchange over the summer, paying out about 35 billion pounds in free shares to members in the process.
In June, Halifax Plc, Britain's largest mortgage lender, paid out 18 billion pounds worth of shares.
Economists had thought consumers borrowed heavily in April and May in anticipation of their windfalls and would pay off debt with their one-off gains afterwards.

Net credit card lending dropped to 250 million pounds in June, from 324 million in May, suggesting some card debt was paid off. But with bank lending climbing fast, it seems most are happy to keep borrowing regardless of the building societies' largesse.

"This data tells us just how buoyant consumers are feeling," said James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Not only are they spending their windfall cash, they are happy to borrow more as well."

Official data released last week showed retail sales rose a healthy 0.6 percent in June. Within that, sales of household goods -- consumer durables such as stereos, televisions and washing machines -- leapt 7.5 percent.
And with numerous low and interest-free deals available, consumers can easily spend in advance of receiving windfall cash.
John O'Sullivan, economist at NatWest Markets, said interest-free credit deals offered little incentive for consumers to spend their cash.
"Windfalls are not being used to pay down accumulated debt," he said. If anything, they are being leveraged to fuel further spending."

David agreed Tuesday's figures showed the unbridled strength of consumer spending. "These numbers are likely to up the pressure for a further hike in base rates, if not at next month's meeting, then soon afterwards."
The Bank of England's monetary policy committee meets next Wednesday and Thursday and the odds on a fourth rate rise in as many months are now finely balanced, analysts said.

Prime Minister Tony Blair acknowledged that interest rates had needed to rise in recent months. He told The Mirror newspaper on Tuesday that higher rates had to be used to "squeeze inflation out of the economy".

Only one factor -- the strength of the pound -- could stay the Bank's hand next week, analysts said. The high exchange rate is punishing British manufacturers, many of which are heavily dependent on export markets.

But so far this week the pound has plunged, dropping below 3.0 marks after an eight-year high above 3.09 a few days ago. If sterling continues to weaken, the central bank will feel no compunction about raising base rates to seven percent from 6.75, analysts said.
